summary: Registers an E.164 Number Mapping (ENUM) service for acct URIs. This lets a telephone number, via DNS, be linked to an account identifier. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone-number lookup now has a line for linking a number to an online account name.

subtitle: Map telephone numbers to online account identifiers using DNS.

tldr.problem: Telephone numbers and online account identifiers exist in separate systems. There is no standard way to look up an account identifier using a phone number via DNS, even though DNS already handles phone number lookups for voice and SMS.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers an Enumservice named 'acct' in the ENUM system, allowing DNS records to link an E.164 telephone number to an acct URI that identifies a user's account at a service provider.
tldr.outcome: Applications like address books, social networks, and phone clients can now discover account identifiers by querying DNS with a phone number, enabling reverse lookup and better routing of mobile communications.

today: RFC 7566 is an Experimental RFC that registers the acct Enumservice. It has not been obsoleted and enables DNS-based lookup of account identifiers from telephone numbers in ENUM.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping) is a DNS-based system for translating telephone numbers like +44 1632 960123 into URIs such as acct:user@example.com. ENUM exists primarily to interconnect systems that rely on telephone numbers with those that use URIs to identify resources.

RFC 7565 defines the acct URI scheme, which identifies a user's account at a service provider using the format acct:localpart@domain. This document registers an Enumservice for the acct scheme, allowing ENUM lookups to return acct URIs associated with a telephone number. This enables applications to discover account identifiers directly from phone numbers using standard DNS queries.
sections.plainLanguage: ENUM is a phone book in DNS. This document adds a new kind of information you can look up: an account name, not just a phone call.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The first major use case is reverse phone lookup. An address book application can issue ENUM queries for acct URIs corresponding to phone numbers, displaying the account identifier and an icon based on the service provider. An endpoint can trigger this during inbound and outbound calls to discover the account associated with the remote party. Businesses and professionals may use ENUM acct records to identify themselves publicly, similar to existing vCard ENUM records.

The second use case involves routing of mobile social communications. The Open Mobile Alliance defines social networking services (SNeW) that let mobile subscribers identified by their MSISDN (Mobile Subscriber Integrated Services Digital Network number) follow each other's activities across service providers. When a user wants to follow another user's social activities, their home SNeW server can use ENUM to resolve the target user's MSISDN to their account URI, identify the target user's service provider, and route the follow request to the correct endpoint. This provides a globally accessible mechanism for discovering account endpoints without relying on proprietary systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Two main ways to use this: first, when you look up a phone number in your address book, also show the person's username. Second, help one social media service find a user on another service by looking up their phone number.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content:
This RFC registers an Enumservice with IANA named 'acct'. The registration follows RFC 6117, which defines the template for registering Enumservices. The registered type is 'acct', matching the acct URI scheme defined in RFC 7565. The Enumservice is classified as Application-Based and Ancillary, and its usage is marked as COMMON.

The registration document (this RFC) serves as the authoritative source for the Enumservice definition. The IANA registry itself is maintained at http://www.iana.org/assignments/enum-services and is the definitive reference for the most current registration details.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA (the number assignment authority for the internet) now has a rule saying "acct" is a valid type of information you can look up alongside a phone number in ENUM.

sections.title: Examples and DNS Considerations
sections.content:
A DNS NAPTR resource record for the phone number +44 1632 960123 using the acct Enumservice might look like:

3.2.1.0.6.9.2.3.6.1.4.4.e164.arpa IN NAPTR 10 100 "u" "E2U+acct" "!^.*$!acct:441632960123@foo.com!" .

The example shows that the userpart can simply replicate the phone number with limited information, or it can contain a full account name like john.doe@example.com.

When applications query for acct records, they may also receive other terminal ENUM records (such as tel: URLs for voice or SMS). If the application chooses to submit ENUM queries for telephone numbers found in those results, it risks entering a query loop if the results point back to numbers already queried. Applications SHOULD detect and abort such loops, potentially by limiting the chain to no more than 5 queries without finding an acct record.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS record format tells where to look up a phone number and what account name to return. You have to be careful not to get stuck looking up the same numbers over and over.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
ENUM is a public, global DNS database. If acct Enumservice records are published in the public e164.arpa tree, they are visible to anyone. Carriers and service providers may choose to publish acct records only in internal ENUM infrastructure accessible only to trusted network elements, limiting privacy risks.

An acct URI itself does not inherently contain personal information but is merely a pointer to an account identifier. Depending on the structure of the URI (for example, if it includes a full name or employer), revealing it could expose personal information. Using anonymous or pseudonymous URIs mitigates this risk.

Unlike a traditional telephone number, an endpoint identified by an acct URI can require requesting entities to provide cryptographic credentials for authentication and authorization before messages are exchanged. This can provide stronger protection from unwanted requests than the PSTN.

The underlying systems that acct URIs point to should implement their own security controls including authentication, integrity, and confidentiality measures to prevent attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing a phone-to-username mapping is public and visible to everyone. You might not want people to know your real name from your phone number, so you can use a fake username or keep the records private.
